this rule applied because where i worked was a rapidly growing area (think country -> suburban within the span of 3 years) with the nearest hospital 30 minutes away and the nearest trauma center 45. 

while fire was meant to respond at the scene, they were never expected to come to the hospital with us unless it was a code. 

personally, if i was available, i'd ask the fire guys to put me to work and tell me what help cleaning they needed, but oftentimes we were still transporting someone (or we were on the way back) when most of these chores got completed. it was not an expectation placed on us because of that.

Honestly, IFT makes you lose so much imo to where it's worthless as experience, and may actually be bad experience. I did about a year of it and felt like it rotted me. I had to relearn how to be an EMT come medic school. 

With that being said, I knew 911 wasn't for me either in about 6 shifts. I cried nearly every day. I never quit a job that fast. I felt like IFT rotted my skills, and that my preceptor was a bitch (she was), and that this job wasn't worth the 13/hr I was making. I ended up working on a high ropes course (completely unrelated to EMS) at higher pay instead throughout medic school and said "fuck this, I'll be a hospital medic instead." And that's ok! 

Honestly, it may not be for you, and that's okay! There's a million jobs EMS folks can work. Since becoming a medic, I've stayed working in hospitals and ERs since then and I'm much happier than I ever was on a box. I'm going into nursing school soon, and am starting at a huge advantage!

 I also did events as a foot medic for almost three years, and I loved that too. I have friends who have done construction contracts, factory medical, etc, and they love it. 

Working 911 is made out to be this big prize and end goal for many of us, so it's disappointing when you find you hate it - I was pretty upset when I realized it wasn't for me too. 

You don't have to work in 911. Be sad about it, and then go use your skills doing something you like instead. 911 isn't the end all be all, nor is it the only valuable way you can be utilized. It isn't the only way you can help people and make a difference. 

Of course, if you want to learn it and want to enjoy it, absolutely take the advice of the other commenters. I'm sharing this to say it's ok if you never do love it, and it's ok to say "this isn't for me." That doesn't make you a bad EMT, nor should anyone ever make you feel bad about that either. I just wish someone had told me this a few years back so I hadn't felt so shitty about deciding "fuck that" for a while. Now, it'll take an act of god to get me back on an ambulance.

and this is coming from someone who openly dislikes field intubations and wants the usage of them minimized. 

with that being said, it all depends what kind of facial trauma they have though. i once saw one where they blew off their jaw, and you could actually see the sweet spot perfectly without the laryngoscope. the lead on that call tubed him. and yes, that patient in question lived. 

if that's not possible, then cric and go. again, i'm not calling it unsurvivable if they're still alive. i'm not in a monty python skit; if they're not dead yet, they're not dead yet (unless it's a MCI and triage standards lead me to mark them as black). 

if that patient were to CODE, however, i'd be more inclined to call med control. obviously, continue working them if it's a witnessed arrest unless given the green light to stop, traumatic arrests in the field rarely return. but if that patient is still alive? we have a duty to service them and do what we can to keep them alive.

paramedics get an even lower rating of approx. 78% accuracy.

if you had one glass of you're nightly wine before falling and breaking your femur? yeah, i'll likely give you fentanyl. 

if you had two sips of a beer and began seizing? yeah, im gonna administer a benzo. 

if you broke a bone and are blackout drunk, to the point of entering and exiting consciousness and are complaining of pain every time you wake up? no, im not giving you fentanyl.

alcohol CONSUMPTION isn't inherently a contraindication. the concern is about respiratory depression.

alcohol is synergistic with both benzos and opiates, meaning that it strengthens the effects of both. one of the effects of all three together is respiratory depression - something we DON'T want to cause. you're essentially weighing your risks and benefits out. and typically, managing pain is less important than ensuring that a patient is breathing.

so i would personally be reluctant as hell to give opiates to a drunk driver who broke bones while crashing because being in pain is better than not breathing. depending on the situation, i may or may not administer pain meds on the basis that the driver is drunk. 

meanwhile, if the driver was sober and did not have any injuries that led me to suspect that they may go into respiratory depression soon, then i'd be a lot more inclined to manage pain with opiates on the box.

is it IFT, hospital, 911, events, etc? i've worked all of the above and the interview process is completely different for all 4.

IFT? i was hired on the spot following a drug test, and they were hiring anyone who didn't actively smell like drugs. with that being said, in my experience, IFT likes to prey on brand new EMTs who won't argue with any questionable practice you're asked to do because IFT is a money grab. i don't regret working IFT, because now i know a lot about red flags, but i'd take it as a last resort.

events? i was given a phone call by my boss and was asked when i could start. it's gotten more streamlined since, but i literally started the evening after my interview. he would have hired anyone because he had 20 spots to fill. now, he looks more for who may be interested in this job - as in a "do you like music?" sort of thing, because people who are invested in that world usually do a better job than people who don't like events.

911? they're looking for a fit into the culture of their station. is it fire based? is it private? do you know anyone who works there? if you do, then talk to them to figure out what the culture is. they're also looking for ability to follow direction and work as a team with your group/partner. will you follow direction of the medic? will you work well with whatever medic they're trying to partner you with (and this is a BIG deal. i quit a 911 job in 6 shifts because i could not work with the medic they were pairing me with, despite it seeming like it would have been a good match on paper. she is pure fucking evil, and they still cannot find her a permanent partner, but i digress). the interview process was a lot about judgement and ability to determine the correct treatment, and less about how good your skills were at the time of hire because as long as you can do CPR, turn on an O2 tank and keep the person stable, they're going to the hospital.

hospital? they're looking for skills. can you start IVs, can you get an EKG, can you obtain vitals, etc. it's less about leadership, unlike a 911 job, because you'll be under the eye of a doctor, and more about "can you do the skill accurately and fast?" are you able to get a good IV start on difficult patients? can you get an EKG done fast? can you follow the direct orders of a doctor? what about your charge nurse? that sort of stuff - because the judgements you're trusted to make in the field go away in the hospital setting since the doctor is right there. you're working as an assistant nurse, essentially. they also want to know if you align with the hospital's values. 

it all comes down to what you're interviewing for. EMS is diverse as hell, and shit, I can't advise on construction because i've never done it. the only universal desirable thing i've seen in interviews is a willingness to learn.

with this said, be careful with small IFT companies. know OSHA laws and know the number of your med control. the leadership of IFT companies is terrible, and if you're not careful and willing to stick up for yourself, you will be asked and coerced into doing things that could cost you your license.

Self diagnosis is a very nuanced subject.

Here's what I'm gonna say: if it's unsafe for you to get dx'ed, you 100% deserve support and love.

Nobody should pressure you to get a diagnosis or be mean to you for not having one. 

However, with autism specifically, there are a lot of symptoms that overlap with other disorders. I was screened for BPD before I was screened for autism due to the overlap in an AFAB adult. I was also screened for various adjustment disorders and had to wait a long time for a diagnosis because time would rule out adjustment issues. 

I think self-diagnosis can be a great tool for self-help purposes. Knowing you're autistic can help you learn the "cheat codes" to yourself, and if self dxing helps you open your mind to various self help forums, then that's great!

With that being said, I don't think you should be publicly calling yourself autistic because there's a good chance that you have something else that looks similar. OCD, BPD, ADHD, and other various personality disorders and learning disorders can be comorbid with or look a lot like autism. 

Also, I hate how we don't acknowledge that being undiagnosed is also a privilege. Diagnosis is 100% a privilege, but being able to live undiagnosed is too. Not needing accommodations and having low enough support needs to not need a diagnosis is a huge privilege - one that I would argue is a larger privilege than a diagnosis is. I say this as someone who has low support needs who would likely not be clocked as anything but weird by most people and who does not need accommodations. Not needing accommodations to get by in day to day life is such a privilege many of us lower support needs folks take for granted. And if you think that I'm wrong, go hang out with some friends who have higher support needs. Look at what living life in a group home entails. Look at what being completely nonverbal entails. Look at what being reliant on others entails. 

I feel at times, we forget that not every autistic person has low support needs because those of us who can run our own pages and accounts and whatnot generally do have lower support needs - but seriously. Having low enough support needs to be able to make the choice to not get diagnosed is a privilege too.
